naxos-sicily.t: The first Greek colony in Sicily, founded by Chalcidians in 734 BCE beneath Mount Etna and destroyed by Dionysius I in 403 BCE.
naxos-sicily.o: According to Thucydides, Chalcidians from Euboea, joined by Naxians from the Aegean, founded Naxos in 734 BCE on the Schisò headland below modern Taormina, led by Theocles. As the first landfall for ships crossing from Greece, it became the starting point for Greek colonisation of the island.
naxos-sicily.r: Naxos was small but symbolically important: its altar of Apollo Archegetes, 'the Founder', was where envoys sailing from Sicily to Greece made sacrifice. Within a few years it sent out settlers to found Leontini and Catana. It grew vines on the slopes of Etna, and its coins with Dionysus and a satyr are celebrated. Hippocrates of Gela subdued it around 495 BCE, and later it was often allied with Athens and Leontini against Syracuse.
naxos-sicily.e: Dionysius I captured Naxos by treachery in 403 BCE, sold its people into slavery and gave its land to the Sicels. In 358 BCE survivors and Sicels founded Tauromenium on the hill above. Excavations at Giardini Naxos have revealed the walls, sanctuaries and street grid.

neustria.t: Western kingdom of the Merovingian Franks, centred on Paris and Soissons, and the long rival of Austrasia.
neustria.o: Neustria, the new western land, took shape after the division of 561, when Chilperic I received Soissons and the lands between the Loire and the Scheldt. It later included Paris, Rouen and Tours.
neustria.r: Chilperic and his queen Fredegund waged a bitter feud with Austrasia's Sigebert I and Brunhild. Their son Chlothar II reunited the Frankish kingdoms in 613. Neustria had a strongly Gallo-Roman population and rich abbeys such as Saint-Denis, and in the 7th century its mayor Ebroin dominated politics.
neustria.e: The Austrasian Pippin of Herstal defeated the Neustrians at Tertry in 687, and Charles Martel finally crushed the Neustrian mayor Ragenfrid in 717 to 719. After 751 Neustria became a region of the Carolingian realm, and the name was later applied to the land between the Seine and the Loire.

novantae.t: People of Galloway in south-west Scotland, named by Ptolemy, whose peninsula and towns faced the Irish Sea.
novantae.o: Ptolemy lists the Novantae in south-western Scotland, giving their name to a peninsula, the Novantarum Promontorium, usually identified with the Rhins of Galloway, and naming two towns, Locopibia and Rerigonium. They grew from Iron Age communities living in duns, crannogs and small forts along the coast and inland valleys of Galloway.
novantae.r: No rulers or written records survive. Agricola's campaigns of about 81 probably brought Roman troops into Galloway, and forts were built at Glenlochar and Gatehouse of Fleet. Their position on the Irish Sea gave them close contact with Ireland and the Isle of Man, and their society was rural and pastoral.
novantae.e: Roman control of the region was brief, and the Novantae disappear from the written record after Ptolemy. Their territory later formed part of British kingdoms of the north, possibly Rheged, before Northumbrian expansion into Galloway in the 7th and 8th centuries.

neutral-moresnet.t: A tiny wedge-shaped territory between Belgium and Prussia, left jointly governed for a century because neither side would give up its zinc mine.
neutral-moresnet.o: After 1815, the Netherlands and Prussia could not agree on the border near Aachen because both wanted the valuable Vieille Montagne zinc mine at Kelmis. In 1816 they left a small triangle of land under joint administration, with Belgium taking the Dutch role after 1830.
neutral-moresnet.r: Neutral Moresnet was run by a mayor and two royal commissioners, one from each neighbour. Its residents paid low taxes and avoided conscription, and the Vieille Montagne company dominated the economy. After the mine was exhausted in 1885, enthusiasts promoted it as a possible Esperanto state called Amikejo, and the territory became known for its gambling and distillery.
neutral-moresnet.e: The Treaty of Versailles of 1919 assigned the territory to the Kingdom of Belgium, effective in 1920. Kelmis, its main village, is now part of Belgium's German-speaking community.

nitiobroges.t: Gallic people of the middle Garonne around Agen, whose king Teutomatus fought for Vercingetorix at Gergovia.
nitiobroges.o: The Nitiobroges lived on the Garonne around Aginnum (Agen), at the border between the Celtic peoples and the Aquitani. Caesar notes that their king Ollovico had been honoured by the Roman Senate as a friend.
nitiobroges.r: They were ruled by kings in Caesar's day. Their land lay on the river route from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic, and their coins circulated widely in south-western Gaul.
nitiobroges.e: Ollovico's son Teutomatus joined Vercingetorix in 52 BCE with cavalry raised in Aquitania; during the attack on Gergovia he escaped from his tent half-dressed on a wounded horse. Under Rome Aginnum became a civitas capital, the origin of Agen.

neapolis.t: Greek 'new city' on the Bay of Naples, founded from Cumae, which kept its Greek speech and customs long after becoming Rome's ally in 326 BCE.
neapolis.o: Cumae founded Neapolis around 470 BCE beside an older settlement, Parthenope, named after a Siren whose tomb was shown there and which became known as Palaepolis, 'old city'. The new town was laid out on a regular grid whose main streets still shape central Naples.
neapolis.r: Neapolis grew through trade and gained importance after Cumae fell to the Campanians around 421 BCE. Athenian settlers are said to have joined it in the 5th century BCE, and it later admitted Campanian families to citizenship. Its coins with a man-headed bull and its torch race in honour of Parthenope are well known. It remained a centre of Greek culture in Campania.
neapolis.e: After a Roman siege in 327–326 BCE, the city made a treaty with Rome on favourable terms and became a loyal naval ally. It kept Greek language and institutions into the Empire, attracting Roman writers such as Virgil, and grew into Naples.

nervii.t: The fiercest of the Belgic peoples, who banned wine and luxuries and almost defeated Caesar at the Battle of the Sabis in 57 BCE.
nervii.o: The Nervii lived in the Hainaut region of modern Belgium and northern France, between the Scheldt and the Sambre. Caesar reports that they forbade merchants and wine, believing luxuries weakened courage, and that they were proud of their Germanic descent.
nervii.r: They had no cavalry to speak of and fought on foot, using thick hedges of bent saplings to block their land against raiders. Their war leader in 57 BCE was Boduognatus.
nervii.e: At the Sabis (probably the Sambre) in 57 BCE they surprised Caesar's camp and were crushed only after a desperate battle. In 54 BCE they besieged Quintus Cicero's winter camp. Under Rome their chief town was Bagacum (Bavay), later Cambrai.

naxos.t: Largest island of the Cyclades, an Archaic marble-working power whose failed siege by Persia in 499 BCE set off the Ionian Revolt.
naxos.o: Naxos was settled by Ionian Greeks in the early Iron Age, building on a long Cycladic and Mycenaean past. Its fertile valleys and white marble made it the leading island of the Cyclades by the 7th century BCE. Tradition linked it with Dionysus and with Ariadne.
naxos.r: Naxian sculptors made colossal kouroi, the Naxian Sphinx at Delphi and the Lions on Delos. The tyrant Lygdamis, helped by Peisistratus, ruled in the mid-6th century BCE, when the great unfinished temple gateway, the Portara, was begun. In 499 BCE Aristagoras of Miletus and the Persians failed to capture Naxos, a fiasco that triggered the Ionian Revolt.
naxos.e: Persia sacked Naxos in 490 BCE. It was the first member to try to leave the Delian League and was subdued c. 470 BCE. Later it joined Hellenistic leagues and passed under Rome by 146 BCE.

northern-ireland.t: The part of the United Kingdom in north-east Ireland, created by partition in 1921 and marked by decades of conflict and a power-sharing peace.
northern-ireland.o: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 created Northern Ireland from six of Ulster's nine counties, where Protestants, mostly unionists, were a majority. Its Parliament opened in June 1921, and it opted out of the Irish Free State in December 1922.
northern-ireland.r: Northern Ireland was governed for fifty years by the Ulster Unionist Party from Stormont, with discrimination against the Catholic, mainly nationalist minority. Belfast was a centre of shipbuilding and linen. The civil rights movement of the late 1960s was followed by the Troubles, which killed about 3,600 people, and direct rule from London from 1972.
northern-ireland.e: The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 established a power-sharing Assembly and Executive and confirmed that Northern Ireland remains in the United Kingdom unless its people vote otherwise.

nagnatae.t: People of north-west Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, who also names a notable town of theirs called Nagnata.
nagnatae.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Nagnatae on the north-west coast of Ireland, roughly in Sligo or north Mayo, and lists a settlement called Nagnata, which he describes as a notable town. His information came from earlier sailors' reports on the Atlantic coast.
nagnatae.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, economy or customs. The identification of Nagnata is disputed; sites around Sligo Bay have been suggested, and some versions of the text spell the people Magnatae, which has led to other proposed meanings. The region was rich in older monuments such as the Carrowmore tombs.
nagnatae.e: No later source mentions the Nagnatae. Their area later lay within the Kingdom of Connacht, ruled by branches of the Connachta dynasties.

nuceria-alfaterna.t: Oscan city of southern Campania that led a league including Pompeii, Herculaneum and Stabiae before becoming an ally of Rome.
nuceria-alfaterna.o: Nuceria Alfaterna, modern Nocera Inferiore, grew in the Sarno valley inland from the Bay of Naples, on the route between Campania and the Gulf of Salerno. Its population was Oscan-speaking by the 5th century BCE, and earlier settlement shows Etruscan and Greek contacts.
nuceria-alfaterna.r: Nuceria headed a league of towns in the Sarno valley and along the coast, including Pompeii, Herculaneum, Stabiae and Surrentum, and issued silver coins in Oscan with the name of the Alfaterni. It controlled a fertile plain producing grain, wine and fruit. Little else is known of its institutions.
nuceria-alfaterna.e: During the Second Samnite War Nuceria fought Rome but submitted in 308 BCE and became an ally on favourable terms. Hannibal destroyed it in 216 BCE for staying loyal to Rome, and it was later rebuilt. In 59 CE a riot between Nucerians and Pompeians in Pompeii's amphitheatre was recorded by Tacitus.

nesiotic-league.t: League of the Cycladic islands centred on Delos, created by Antigonus I and used by Hellenistic kings to control the Aegean.
nesiotic-league.o: Around 314 BCE Antigonus I Monophthalmus, seeking support in the Aegean against rival successors of Alexander, organised the islands of the Cyclades into a league with its headquarters at the sanctuary of Apollo on Delos. Members celebrated festivals named after Antigonus and his son Demetrius.
nesiotic-league.r: Delegates of the islands met in a federal council (synedrion) on Delos, voted honours for royal patrons and handled common affairs, but real power lay with the protecting king. After the collapse of Demetrius, the league passed under Ptolemaic control in the 280s BCE; officials called nesiarchs and Philocles, king of Sidon, acted for Ptolemy II, and the islanders founded the Ptolemaia festival.
nesiotic-league.e: Ptolemaic power in the Aegean waned in the mid-3rd century BCE and the league faded. It was revived around 200 BCE under Rhodian leadership, but ended in 167 BCE when Rome gave Delos to Athens and declared it a free port, ending Rhodian dominance.

neapolitan-republic-1647-1648.t: A short-lived republic born of Masaniello's revolt against Spanish taxes in Naples, which briefly invited a French duke as its leader.
neapolitan-republic-1647-1648.o: In July 1647 a new tax on fruit sparked a rising in Naples led by the fisherman Tommaso Aniello, known as Masaniello. He was murdered within days, but the revolt spread, and in October 1647 the gunsmith Gennaro Annese proclaimed a republic independent of Spanish rule in the Kingdom of Naples.
neapolitan-republic-1647-1648.r: The rebels held most of the city while Spanish forces kept the castles and the fleet bombarded the town. They invited Henry II, Duke of Guise, a French claimant to the Angevin inheritance, who arrived in November and took the title Duke of the Republic. Quarrels between Guise, Annese and the nobles, and limited French support, weakened the regime, and the provinces were divided between rebels and barons.
neapolitan-republic-1647-1648.e: In April 1648, while Guise was outside the city, Spanish troops under Don John of Austria retook Naples with the help of Annese. Guise was captured, and Spanish rule was restored.

namnetes.t: Gallic people of the Loire estuary, allies of the Veneti against Caesar, who gave their name to the city of Nantes.
namnetes.o: The Namnetes lived on the north bank of the lower Loire, with a port called Condevicnum or Portus Namnetum on the site of Nantes. Strabo and Ptolemy place them between the Veneti and the Pictones, and Greek writers knew the Loire mouth as a trading point for Atlantic tin, linked to the earlier port of Corbilo.
namnetes.r: Little is known of their government. They took part in the Atlantic trade of the Armorican peoples and struck gold and silver coins of Armorican style.
namnetes.e: In 56 BCE the Namnetes sent help to the Veneti in their naval war against Caesar and shared in their defeat. Under Rome their port grew into the town of Condevicnum, renamed after the people as Namnetes, the origin of the name Nantes.

northern-march.t: A Saxon frontier march east of the Elbe, lost to the Slavs in 983 and revived as the territory that became the March of Brandenburg.
northern-march.o: When Margrave Gero died in 965 his huge march was split, and the northern part, between the Elbe and the Oder north of the Havel, became the Northern March. Its first margrave was Dietrich of Haldensleben, who ruled over the Hevelli and Lutician Slavs.
northern-march.r: The Northern March was a military frontier, defended by castles and supported by the bishoprics of Havelberg and Brandenburg. Dietrich's harsh rule helped provoke the Great Slav Rising of 983, after which German power collapsed east of the Elbe and the margraves held only the Altmark on the west bank, around Salzwedel and Stendal.
northern-march.e: In 1134 Lothair III granted the Northern March to the Ascanian Albert the Bear. After he secured Brandenburg in 1157, he took the title of Margrave of Brandenburg. The old march, with the Altmark as its western core, became part of the Margraviate of Brandenburg.
